L60@P4: I
L61@P4: What is the problem we wish to solve when we try to construct a rational economic
L62@P4: order? On certain familiar assumptions the answer is simple enough. If we possess all
L63@P4: the relevant information, if we can start out from a given system of preferences, and if
L64@P4: we command complete knowledge of available means, the problem which remains is
L65@P4: purely one of logic. That is, the answer to the question of what is the best use of the
L66@P4: available means is implicit in our assumptions. The conditions which the solution of
L67@P4: this optimum problem must satisfy have been fully worked out and can be stated best
L68@P4: in mathematical form: put at their briefest, they are that the marginal rates of
L69@P4: substitution between any two commodities or factors must be the same in all their
L70@P4: different uses.
L71@P4: This, however, is emphatically not the economic problem which society faces. And
L72@P4: the economic calculus which we have developed to solve this logical problem, though
L73@P4: an important step toward the solution of the economic problem of society, does not
L74@P4: yet provide an answer to it. The reason for this is that the “data” from which the
L75@P4: economic calculus starts are never for the whole society “given” to a single mind
L76@P4: which could work out the implications and can never be so given.
L77@P4: The peculiar character of the problem of a rational economic order is determined
L78@P4: precisely by the fact that the knowledge of the circumstances of which we must make
L79@P4: use never exists in concentrated or integrated form but solely as the dispersed bits of
L80@P4: incomplete and frequently contradictory knowledge which all the separate individuals
L81@P4: possess. The economic problem of society is thus not merely a problem of how to
L82@P4: allocate “given” resources—if “given” is taken to mean given to a single mind which
L83@P4: deliberately solves the problem set by these “data.” It is rather a problem of how to
L84@P4: secure the best use of resources known to any of the members of society, for ends
L85@P4: whose relative importance only these individuals know. Or, to put it briefly, it is a
L86@P4: problem of the utilization of knowledge which is not given to anyone in its totality.
L87@P4: This character of the fundamental problem has, I am afraid, been obscured rather than
L88@P4: illuminated by many of the recent refinements of economic theory, particularly by
L89@P4: many of the uses made of mathematics. Though the problem with which I want
L90@P4: primarily to deal in this paper is the problem of a rational economic organization, I
L91@P4: shall in its course be led again and again to point to its close connections with certain
L92@P4: methodological questions. Many of the points I wish to make are indeed conclusions
L93@P4: toward which diverse paths of reasoning have unexpectedly converged. But, as I now
L94@P4: see these problems, this is no accident. It seems to me that many of the current
L95@P4: disputes with regard to both economic theory and economic policy have their
L96@P4: common origin in a misconception about the nature of the economic problem of

L99@P5: phenomena of the habits of thought we have developed in dealing with the
L100@P5: phenomena of nature.

L103@P6: II
L104@P6: In ordinary language we describe by the word “planning” the complex of interrelated
L105@P6: decisions about the allocation of our available resources. All economic activity is in
L106@P6: this sense planning; and in any society in which many people collaborate, this
L107@P6: planning, whoever does it, will in some measure have to be based on knowledge
L108@P6: which, in the first instance, is not given to the planner but to somebody else, which
L109@P6: somehow will have to be conveyed to the planner. The various ways in which the
L110@P6: knowledge on which people base their plans is communicated to them is the crucial
L111@P6: problem for any theory explaining the economic process, and the problem of what is
L112@P6: the best way of utilizing knowledge initially dispersed among all the people is at least
L113@P6: one of the main problems of economic policy—or of designing an efficient economic
L114@P6: system.
L115@P6: The answer to this question is closely connected with that other question which arises
L116@P6: here, that of who is to do the planning. It is about this question that all the dispute
L117@P6: about “economic planning” centers. This is not a dispute about whether planning is to
L118@P6: be done or not. It is a dispute as to whether planning is to be done centrally, by one
L119@P6: authority for the whole economic system, or is to be divided among many individuals.
L120@P6: Planning in the specific sense in which the term is used in contemporary controversy
L121@P6: necessarily means central planning—direction of the whole economic system
L122@P6: according to one unified plan. Competition, on the other hand, means decentralized
L123@P6: planning by many separate persons. The halfway house between the two, about which
L124@P6: many people talk but which few like when they see it, is the delegation of planning to
L125@P6: organized industries, or, in other words, monopoly.
L126@P6: Which of these systems is likely to be more efficient depends mainly on the question
L127@P6: under which of them we can expect that fuller use will be made of the existing
L128@P6: knowledge. And this, in turn, depends on whether we are more likely to succeed in
L129@P6: putting at the disposal of a single central authority all the knowledge which ought to
L130@P6: be used but which is initially dispersed among many different individuals, or in
L131@P6: conveying to the individuals such additional knowledge as they need in order to
L132@P6: enable them to fit their plans with those of others.
L133@P6: Online Library of Liberty: “The Use of Knowledge in Society”

L135@P7: III
L136@P7: It will at once be evident that on this point the position will be different with respect
L137@P7: to different kinds of knowledge; and the answer to our question will therefore largely
L138@P7: turn on the relative importance of the different kinds of knowledge; those more likely
L139@P7: to be at the disposal of particular individuals and those which we should with greater
L140@P7: confidence expect to find in the possession of an authority made up of suitably chosen
L141@P7: experts. If it is today so widely assumed that the latter will be in a better position, this
L142@P7: is because one kind of knowledge, namely, scientific knowledge, occupies now so
L143@P7: prominent a place in public imagination that we tend to forget that it is not the only
L144@P7: kind that is relevant. It may be admitted that, as far as scientific knowledge is
L145@P7: concerned, a body of suitably chosen experts may be in the best position to command
L146@P7: all the best knowledge available—though this is of course merely shifting the
L147@P7: difficulty to the problem of selecting the experts. What I wish to point out is that, even
L148@P7: assuming that this problem can be readily solved, it is only a small part of the wider
L149@P7: problem.
L150@P7: Today it is almost heresy to suggest that scientific knowledge is not the sum of all
L151@P7: knowledge. But a little reflection will show that there is beyond question a body of
L152@P7: very important but unorganized knowledge which cannot possibly be called scientific
L153@P7: in the sense of knowledge of general rules: the knowledge of the particular
L154@P7: circumstances of time and place. It is with respect to this that practically every
L155@P7: individual has some advantage over all others because he possesses unique
L156@P7: information of which beneficial use might be made, but of which use can be made
L157@P7: only if the decisions depending on it are left to him or are made with his active
L158@P7: coöperation. We need to remember only how much we have to learn in any
L159@P7: occupation after we have completed our theoretical training, how big a part of our
L160@P7: working life we spend learning particular jobs, and how valuable an asset in all walks
L161@P7: of life is knowledge of people, of local conditions, and of special circumstances. To
L162@P7: know of and put to use a machine not fully employed, or somebody's skill which
L163@P7: could be better utilized, or to be aware of a surplus stock which can be drawn upon
L164@P7: during an interruption of supplies, is socially quite as useful as the knowledge of
L165@P7: better alternative techniques. And the shipper who earns his living from using
L166@P7: otherwise empty or half-filled journeys of tramp-steamers, or the estate agent whose
L167@P7: whole knowledge is almost exclusively one of temporary opportunities, or the
L168@P7: arbitrageur who gains from local differences of commodity prices, are all performing
L169@P7: eminently useful functions based on special knowledge of circumstances of the
L170@P7: fleeting moment not known to others.
L171@P7: It is a curious fact that this sort of knowledge should today be generally regarded with
L172@P7: a kind of contempt and that anyone who by such knowledge gains an advantage over
L173@P7: somebody better equipped with theoretical or technical knowledge is thought to have
L174@P7: acted almost disreputably. To gain an advantage from better knowledge of facilities of
L175@P7: communication or transport is sometimes regarded as almost dishonest, although it is
L176@P7: quite as important that society make use of the best opportunities in this respect as in
L177@P7: using the latest scientific discoveries. This prejudice has in a considerable measure
L178@P7: Online Library of Liberty: “The Use of Knowledge in Society”

L180@P8: production. Even economists who regard themselves as definitely immune to the
L181@P8: crude materialist fallacies of the past constantly commit the same mistake where
L182@P8: activities directed toward the acquisition of such practical knowledge are
L183@P8: concerned—apparently because in their scheme of things all such knowledge is
L184@P8: supposed to be “given.” The common idea now seems to be that all such knowledge
L185@P8: should as a matter of course be readily at the command of everybody, and the
L186@P8: reproach of irrationality leveled against the existing economic order is frequently
L187@P8: based on the fact that it is not so available. This view disregards the fact that the
L188@P8: method by which such knowledge can be made as widely available as possible is
L189@P8: precisely the problem to which we have to find an answer.

L192@P9: IV
L193@P9: If it is fashionable today to minimize the importance of the knowledge of the
L194@P9: particular circumstances of time and place, this is closely connected with the smaller
L195@P9: importance which is now attached to change as such. Indeed, there are few points on
L196@P9: which the assumptions made (usually only implicitly) by the “planners” differ from
L197@P9: those of their opponents as much as with regard to the significance and frequency of
L198@P9: changes which will make substantial alterations of production plans necessary. Of
L199@P9: course, if detailed economic plans could be laid down for fairly long periods in
L200@P9: advance and then closely adhered to, so that no further economic decisions of
L201@P9: importance would be required, the task of drawing up a comprehensive plan
L202@P9: governing all economic activity would be much less formidable.
L203@P9: It is, perhaps, worth stressing that economic problems arise always and only in
L204@P9: consequence of change. So long as things continue as before, or at least as they were
L205@P9: expected to, there arise no new problems requiring a decision, no need to form a new
L206@P9: plan. The belief that changes, or at least day-to-day adjustments, have become less
L207@P9: important in modern times implies the contention that economic problems also have
L208@P9: become less important. This belief in the decreasing importance of change is, for that
L209@P9: reason, usually held by the same people who argue that the importance of economic
L210@P9: considerations has been driven into the background by the growing importance of
L211@P9: technological knowledge.
L212@P9: Is it true that, with the elaborate apparatus of modern production, economic decisions
L213@P9: are required only at long intervals, as when a new factory is to be erected or a new
L214@P9: process to be introduced? Is it true that, once a plant has been built, the rest is all more
L215@P9: or less mechanical, determined by the character of the plant, and leaving little to be
L216@P9: changed in adapting to the ever-changing circumstances of the moment?
L217@P9: The fairly widespread belief in the affirmative is not, as far as I can ascertain, borne
L218@P9: out by the practical experience of the businessman. In a competitive industry at any
L219@P9: rate—and such an industry alone can serve as a test—the task of keeping cost from
L220@P9: rising requires constant struggle, absorbing a great part of the energy of the manager.
L221@P9: How easy it is for an inefficient manager to dissipate the differentials on which
L222@P9: profitability rests, and that it is possible, with the same technical facilities, to produce
L223@P9: with a great variety of costs, are among the commonplaces of business experience
L224@P9: which do not seem to be equally familiar in the study of the economist. The very
L225@P9: strength of the desire, constantly voiced by producers and engineers, to be allowed to
L226@P9: proceed untrammeled by considerations of money costs, is eloquent testimony to the
L227@P9: extent to which these factors enter into their daily work.
L228@P9: One reason why economists are increasingly apt to forget about the constant small
L229@P9: changes which make up the whole economic picture is probably their growing
L230@P9: preoccupation with statistical aggregates, which show a very much greater stability
L231@P9: than the movements of the detail. The comparative stability of the aggregates cannot,
L232@P9: however, be accounted for—as the statisticians occasionally seem to be inclined to
L233@P9: Online Library of Liberty: “The Use of Knowledge in Society”
L234@P9-10: PLL v6.0 (generated September, 2011) 10 http://oll.libertyfund.org/title/92do—by the “law of large numbers” or the mutual compensation of random changes.
L235@P10: The number of elements with which we have to deal is not large enough for such
L236@P10: accidental forces to produce stability. The continuous flow of goods and services is
L237@P10: maintained by constant deliberate adjustments, by new dispositions made every day in
L238@P10: the light of circumstances not known the day before, by B stepping in at once when A
L239@P10: fails to deliver. Even the large and highly mechanized plant keeps going largely
L240@P10: because of an environment upon which it can draw for all sorts of unexpected needs;
L241@P10: tiles for its roof, stationery for its forms, and all the thousand and one kinds of
L242@P10: equipment in which it cannot be self-contained and which the plans for the operation
L243@P10: of the plant require to be readily available in the market.
L244@P10: This is, perhaps, also the point where I should briefly mention the fact that the sort of
L245@P10: knowledge with which I have been concerned is knowledge of the kind which by its
L246@P10: nature cannot enter into statistics and therefore cannot be conveyed to any central
L247@P10: authority in statistical form. The statistics which such a central authority would have
L248@P10: to use would have to be arrived at precisely by abstracting from minor differences
L249@P10: between the things, by lumping together, as resources of one kind, items which differ
L250@P10: as regards location, quality, and other particulars, in a way which may be very
L251@P10: significant for the specific decision. It follows from this that central planning based on
L252@P10: statistical information by its nature cannot take direct account of these circumstances
L253@P10: of time and place and that the central planner will have to find some way or other in
L254@P10: which the decisions depending on them can be left to the “man on the spot.”
L255@P10: Online Library of Liberty: “The Use of Knowledge in Society”

L257@P11: V
L258@P11: If we can agree that the economic problem of society is mainly one of rapid
L259@P11: adaptation to changes in the particular circumstances of time and place, it would seem
L260@P11: to follow that the ultimate decisions must be left to the people who are familiar with
L261@P11: these circumstances, who know directly of the relevant changes and of the resources
L262@P11: immediately available to meet them. We cannot expect that this problem will be
L263@P11: solved by first communicating all this knowledge to a central board which, after
L264@P11: integrating all knowledge, issues its orders. We must solve it by some form of
L265@P11: decentralization. But this answers only part of our problem. We need decentralization
L266@P11: because only thus can we insure that the knowledge of the particular circumstances of
L267@P11: time and place will be promptly used. But the “man on the spot” cannot decide solely
L268@P11: on the basis of his limited but intimate knowledge of the facts of his immediate
L269@P11: surroundings. There still remains the problem of communicating to him such further
L270@P11: information as he needs to fit his decisions into the whole pattern of changes of the
L271@P11: larger economic system.
L272@P11: How much knowledge does he need to do so successfully? Which of the events which
L273@P11: happen beyond the horizon of his immediate knowledge are of relevance to his
L274@P11: immediate decision, and how much of them need he know?
L275@P11: There is hardly anything that happens anywhere in the world that might not have an
L276@P11: effect on the decision he ought to make. But he need not know of these events as
L277@P11: such, nor of all their effects. It does not matter for him why at the particular moment
L278@P11: more screws of one size than of another are wanted, why paper bags are more readily
L279@P11: available than canvas bags, or why skilled labor, or particular machine tools, have for
L280@P11: the moment become more difficult to obtain. All that is significant for him is how
L281@P11: much more or less difficult to procure they have become compared with other things
L282@P11: with which he is also concerned, or how much more or less urgently wanted are the
L283@P11: alternative things he produces or uses. It is always a question of the relative
L284@P11: importance of the particular things with which he is concerned, and the causes which
L285@P11: alter their relative importance are of no interest to him beyond the effect on those
L286@P11: concrete things of his own environment.
L287@P11: It is in this connection that what I have called the “economic calculus” proper helps
L288@P11: us, at least by analogy, to see how this problem can be solved, and in fact is being
L289@P11: solved, by the price system. Even the single controlling mind, in possession of all the
L290@P11: data for some small, self-contained economic system, would not—every time some
L291@P11: small adjustment in the allocation of resources had to be made—go explicitly through
L292@P11: all the relations between ends and means which might possibly be affected. It is
L293@P11: indeed the great contribution of the pure logic of choice that it has demonstrated
L294@P11: conclusively that even such a single mind could solve this kind of problem only by
L295@P11: constructing and constantly using rates of equivalence (or “values,” or “marginal rates
L296@P11: of substitution"), i.e., by attaching to each kind of scarce resource a numerical index
L297@P11: which cannot be derived from any property possessed by that particular thing, but
L298@P11: which reflects, or in which is condensed, its significance in view of the whole meansOnline Library of Liberty: “The Use of Knowledge in Society”
L299@P11-12: PLL v6.0 (generated September, 2011) 12 http://oll.libertyfund.org/title/92end structure. In any small change he will have to consider only these quantitative
L300@P12: indices (or “values") in which all the relevant information is concentrated; and, by
L301@P12: adjusting the quantities one by one, he can appropriately rearrange his dispositions
L302@P12: without having to solve the whole puzzle ab initio or without needing at any stage to
L303@P12: survey it at once in all its ramifications.
L304@P12: Fundamentally, in a system in which the knowledge of the relevant facts is dispersed
L305@P12: among many people, prices can act to coördinate the separate actions of different
L306@P12: people in the same way as subjective values help the individual to coördinate the parts
L307@P12: of his plan. It is worth contemplating for a moment a very simple and commonplace
L308@P12: instance of the action of the price system to see what precisely it accomplishes.
L309@P12: Assume that somewhere in the world a new opportunity for the use of some raw
L310@P12: material, say, tin, has arisen, or that one of the sources of supply of tin has been
L311@P12: eliminated. It does not matter for our purpose—and it is very significant that it does
L312@P12: not matter—which of these two causes has made tin more scarce. All that the users of
L313@P12: tin need to know is that some of the tin they used to consume is now more profitably
L314@P12: employed elsewhere and that, in consequence, they must economize tin. There is no
L315@P12: need for the great majority of them even to know where the more urgent need has
L316@P12: arisen, or in favor of what other needs they ought to husband the supply. If only some
L317@P12: of them know directly of the new demand, and switch resources over to it, and if the
L318@P12: people who are aware of the new gap thus created in turn fill it from still other
L319@P12: sources, the effect will rapidly spread throughout the whole economic system and
L320@P12: influence not only all the uses of tin but also those of its substitutes and the substitutes
L321@P12: of these substitutes, the supply of all the things made of tin, and their substitutes, and
L322@P12: so on; and all his without the great majority of those instrumental in bringing about
L323@P12: these substitutions knowing anything at all about the original cause of these changes.
L324@P12: The whole acts as one market, not because any of its members survey the whole field,
L325@P12: but because their limited individual fields of vision sufficiently overlap so that
L326@P12: through many intermediaries the relevant information is communicated to all. The
L327@P12: mere fact that there is one price for any commodity—or rather that local prices are
L328@P12: connected in a manner determined by the cost of transport, etc.—brings about the
L329@P12: solution which (it is just conceptually possible) might have been arrived at by one
L330@P12: single mind possessing all the information which is in fact dispersed among all the
L331@P12: people involved in the process.
L332@P12: Online Library of Liberty: “The Use of Knowledge in Society”

L334@P13: VI
L335@P13: We must look at the price system as such a mechanism for communicating
L336@P13: information if we want to understand its real function—a function which, of course, it
L337@P13: fulfils less perfectly as prices grow more rigid. (Even when quoted prices have
L338@P13: become quite rigid, however, the forces which would operate through changes in price
L339@P13: still operate to a considerable extent through changes in the other terms of the
L340@P13: contract.) The most significant fact about this system is the economy of knowledge
L341@P13: with which it operates, or how little the individual participants need to know in order
L342@P13: to be able to take the right action. In abbreviated form, by a kind of symbol, only the
L343@P13: most essential information is passed on and passed on only to those concerned. It is
L344@P13: more than a metaphor to describe the price system as a kind of machinery for
L345@P13: registering change, or a system of telecommunications which enables individual
L346@P13: producers to watch merely the movement of a few pointers, as an engineer might
L347@P13: watch the hands of a few dials, in order to adjust their activities to changes of which

L349@P13: Of course, these adjustments are probably never “perfect” in the sense in which the
L350@P13: economist conceives of them in his equilibrium analysis. But I fear that our theoretical
L351@P13: habits of approaching the problem with the assumption of more or less perfect
L352@P13: knowledge on the part of almost everyone has made us somewhat blind to the true
L353@P13: function of the price mechanism and led us to apply rather misleading standards in
L354@P13: judging its efficiency. The marvel is that in a case like that of a scarcity of one raw
L355@P13: material, without an order being issued, without more than perhaps a handful of

L360@P13: rates will always be maintained at the same constant or “normal” level.

L0@P0: Information and Economics:
L1@P0: A Critique of Hayek
L2@P0: Allin F. Cottrell and W. Paul Cockshott
L3@P0: October, 1994
L4@P0: 1 introduction
L5@P0: Neither the theoretical arguments put forward
L6@P0: in the West, nor the fact of the collapse of
L7@P0: Soviet socialism, historic landmark as it undoubtedly is, warrant the belief that socialist
L8@P0: economic planning tout court is an untenable
L9@P0: notion whose time has passed. Indeed, modern developments in information technology
L10@P0: open up the possibility of a planning system
L11@P0: that could outperform the market in terms of
L12@P0: efficiency (in meeting human needs) as well
L13@P0: as equity. Such are the claims that we have
L14@P0: defended in a number of recent publications,
L15@P0: designed to re-open a debate over socialist
L16@P0: economics.1 We do not expect that our ideas
L17@P0: will meet with immediate political success,
L18@P0: but we do venture to hope that open-minded
L19@P0: economists will consider our economic arguments on their merits.
L20@P0: We do not intend to reiterate our general
L21@P0: arguments in favour of planning here. Our object is to refute the objections to socialist plan1Our ideas were first presented in Cockshott and
L22@P0: Cottrell (1989), and are set out most fully in Cockshott
L23@P0: and Cottrell (1993). Cottrell and Cockshott (1993a)
L24@P0: re-examines the historic socialist calculation debate,
L25@P0: with emphasis on the arguments of Mises and Lange.
L26@P0: In Cottrell and Cockshott (1993b) we stress the differences between our proposals and the system that
L27@P0: existed in the Soviet Union. Technical details of the
L28@P0: algorithm we propose for short- to medium-term planning are spelled out in Cockshott (1990).
L29@P0: ning put forward by Hayek in his classic article ‘The Use of Knowledge in Society’ (1945).
L30@P0: The relevance of such an argument to the readership of this journal might be questioned.
L31@P0: Doesn’t Hayek lie outside of the mainstream
L32@P0: of British (increasingly, Anglo-American) professional economics, with its dual roots in Marshallian pragmatism and the formal general
L33@P0: equilibrium theory of the Lausanne school?
L34@P0: Wasn’t Hayek’s defence of the market always
L35@P0: a bit too strident and doctrinaire to suit the
L36@P0: sensibilities of a profession that (in Britain
L37@P0: at any rate) has traditionally had a broadly
L38@P0: social-democratic outlook? Maybe so, but it is
L39@P0: our impression that Hayek’s star is on the rise
L40@P0: in the post-Communist world, and that even
L41@P0: those who baulk at his extreme enthusiasm for
L42@P0: the unfettered market are often quite ready to
L43@P0: see his arguments used to bury any form of
L44@P0: thorough-going socialism.
L45@P0: And so to business. We offer below an exposition and point-by-point contestation of the
L46@P0: ideas in Hayek (1945). We should make it clear
L47@P0: that some, though by no means all, of our criticisms of Hayek are anachronistic—that is, they
L48@P0: depend on advances in information technology
L49@P0: that have taken place since Hayek wrote. We
L50@P0: think this is justified for two reasons. First,
L51@P0: Hayek clearly thought he was putting forward a very general argument, which he did
L52@P0: not expect to see undermined by technological
L53@P0: change. Second, Hayek’s followers (e.g. Lavoie,
L54@P0-1: 11985) continue to support his arguments of
L55@P1: several decades ago, and to assert that developments in information technology are largely
L56@P1: beside the point.
L57@P1: In our exposition of Hayek we try to balance concision with the need to produce a sufficiently full and fair account to obviate the
L58@P1: suspicion that we may be attacking a straw
L59@P1: man. We begin with a brief summary of the
L60@P1: philosophical views that inform the argument
L61@P1: of ‘The Use of Knowledge in Society’, which
L62@P1: are spelled out more fully in The CounterRevolution of Science (Hayek, 1955).
L63@P1: 2 hayek’s argument outlined
L64@P1: 2.1 The philosophical
L65@P1: background
L66@P1: In The Counter Revolution of Science Hayek
L67@P1: is concerned to contrast the natural and social
L68@P1: sciences, whose relation to their subject matter, he claims, is fundamentally different. In
L69@P1: the natural sciences, advances involve recognising that things are not what they seem.
L70@P1: Science dissolves the immediate categories of
L71@P1: subjective experience and replaces them with
L72@P1: underlying, often hidden, causes. The study of
L73@P1: society on the other hand has to take as its
L74@P1: raw material the ideas and beliefs of people in
L75@P1: society. The facts studied by social science
L76@P1: differ from the facts of the physical sciences in being beliefs or opinions held by
L77@P1: particular people, beliefs which as such
L78@P1: are our data, irrespective of whether
L79@P1: they are true or false, and which, moreover, we cannot directly observe in the
L80@P1: minds of people but which we can recognise from what they say or do merely because we have ourselves a mind similar
L81@P1: to theirs. (Hayek, 1955, p. 28)
L82@P1: He argues that there is an irreducible subjective element to the subject mater of the social sciences which was absent in the physical
L83@P1: sciences.
L84@P1: [M]ost of the objects of social or human
L85@P1: action are not “objective facts” in the
L86@P1: special narrow sense in which the term
L87@P1: is used in the Sciences and contrasted
L88@P1: to “opinions”, and they cannot at all be
L89@P1: defined in physical terms. So far as human actions are concerned, things are
L90@P1: what the acting people think they are.
L91@P1: (Hayek, 1955, pp. 27–27)
L92@P1: His paradigm for the social or moral sciences
L93@P1: is that society must be understood in terms of
L94@P1: men’s conscious reflected actions, it being assumed that people are constantly consciously
L95@P1: choosing between different possible courses of
L96@P1: action. Any collective phenomena must thus
L97@P1: be conceived of as the unintended outcome of
L98@P1: the decisions of individual conscious actors.
L99@P1: This imposes a fundamental dichotomy between the study of nature and of society, since
L100@P1: in dealing with natural phenomena it may be
L101@P1: reasonable to suppose that the individual scientist can know all the relevant information,
L102@P1: while in the social context this condition cannot possibly be met.
L103@P1: 2.2 The basic economic problem
L104@P1: From this philosophical ground Hayek (1945)
L105@P1: poses the question: ‘What is the problem we
L106@P1: wish to solve when we try to construct a rational economic order?’
L107@P1: He continues:
L108@P1: On certain familiar assumptions the answer is simple enough. If we possess all
L109@P1: the relevant information, if we can start
L110@P1: out from a given system of preferences
L111@P1: and if we command complete knowledge
L112@P1: of available means, the problem which
L113@P1: remains is purely one of logic. That is,
L114@P1-2: 2the answer to the question of what is
L115@P2: the best use of the available means is
L116@P2: implicit in our assumptions. The conditions which the solution of this optimum
L117@P2: problem must satisfy have been fully
L118@P2: worked out and can be stated best in
L119@P2: mathematical form: put at their briefest,
L120@P2: they are that the marginal rates of substitution between any two commodities
L121@P2: or factors must be the same in all their
L122@P2: different uses. (Hayek, 1945, p. 519)
L123@P2: He immediately makes it clear, however,
L124@P2: that the ‘familiar assumptions’ upon which the
L125@P2: above approach is predicated are quite unreal.
L126@P2: This, however, is emphatically not the
L127@P2: economic problem which society faces
L128@P2: . . . The reason for this is that the data
L129@P2: from which the economic calculus starts
L130@P2: are never for the whole society given to
L131@P2: a single mind which could work out the
L132@P2: implications, and can never be so given.
L133@P2: (ibid.)
L134@P2: Hayek then spells out his own perspective
L135@P2: on the nature of the problem:
L136@P2: The peculiar character of the problem of
L137@P2: a rational economic order is determined
L138@P2: precisely by the fact that the knowledge
L139@P2: of the circumstances of which we must
L140@P2: make use never exists in concentrated
L141@P2: or integrated form, but solely as the dispersed bits of incomplete and frequently
L142@P2: contradictory knowledge which all the
L143@P2: separate individuals possess. (ibid.)
L144@P2: The true problem is therefore “how to secure the best use of resources known to any
L145@P2: of the members of society, for ends whose relative importance only these individuals know”
L146@P2: (Hayek, 1945, p. 520, emphasis added). That
L147@P2: this is not generally understood, Hayek claims,
L148@P2: is an effect of naturalism or scientism, that is
L149@P2: “the erroneous transfer to social phenomena
L150@P2: of the habits of thought we have developed in
L151@P2: dealing with the phenomena of nature” (ibid.).
L152@P2: 2.3 Against centralisation
L153@P2: The point at issue between Hayek and the
L154@P2: proponents of socialist economic planning is
L155@P2: not “whether planning is to be done or not”.
L156@P2: Rather it is “whether planning is to be done
L157@P2: centrally, by one authority for the whole economic system, or is to be divided among many
L158@P2: individuals” (Hayek, 1945, pp. 520–21). The
L159@P2: latter case is nothing other than market competition, which “means decentralized planning
L160@P2: by many separate persons” (Hayek, 1945, p.
L161@P2: 521). And the relative efficiency of the two alternatives hinges on
L162@P2: whether we are more likely to succeed in
L163@P2: putting at the disposal of a single central authority all the knowledge which
L164@P2: ought to be used but which is initially
L165@P2: dispersed . . . or in conveying to individuals such additional knowledge as they
L166@P2: need in order to fit their plans in with
L167@P2: those of others. (ibid.)
L168@P2: The next step in Hayek’s argument involves distinguishing two different kinds of
L169@P2: knowledge: scientific knowledge (understood
L170@P2: as knowledge of general laws) versus “unorganized knowledge” or “knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place”. The
L171@P2: former, he says, may be susceptible of centralization via a “body of suitably chosen experts”
L172@P2: (Hayek, 1945, p. 521) but the latter is a different matter.
L173@P2: [P]ractically every individual has some
L174@P2: advantage over others in that he possesses unique information of which beneficial use might be made, but of which
L175@P2: use can be made only if the decisions
L176@P2: depending on it are left to him or
L177@P2: are made with his active cooperation.
L178@P2: (Hayek, 1945, pp. 521–22)
L179@P2: Hayek is thinking here of “knowledge of people, of local conditions, and special circumstances” (Hayek, 1945, p. 522), e.g., of the fact
L180@P2-3: 3that a certain machine is not fully employed,
L181@P3: or of a skill that could be better utilized. He
L182@P3: also cites the sort of specific, localised knowledge relied upon by shippers and arbitrageurs.
L183@P3: He claims that this sort of knowledge is often
L184@P3: seriously undervalued by those who consider
L185@P3: general scientific knowledge as paradigmatic.
L186@P3: 2.4 The importance of change
L187@P3: Closely related, in Hayek’s mind, to the undervaluation of knowledge of local and specific
L188@P3: factors is underestimation of the role of change
L189@P3: in the economy. One key difference between
L190@P3: advocates and critics of planning concerns
L191@P3: the significance and frequency of
L192@P3: changes which will make substantial alterations of production plans necessary.
L193@P3: Of course, if detailed economic plans
L194@P3: could be laid down for fairly long periods in advance and then closely adhered to, so that no further economic decisions of importance would be required,
L195@P3: the task of drawing up a comprehensive plan governing all economic activity would appear much less formidable.
L196@P3: (Hayek, 1945, p. 523)
L197@P3: Hayek ascribes to his opponents the idea
L198@P3: that economically-relevant change is something that occurs at discrete intervals and on
L199@P3: a fairly long time-scale, and that in between
L200@P3: such changes the management of the productive system is a more or less mechanical task.
L201@P3: As against this, he cites, for instance, the problem of keeping cost from rising in a competitive industry, which requires considerable dayto-day managerial energy, and he emphasises
L202@P3: the fact that the same technical facilities may
L203@P3: be operated at widely differing cost levels by
L204@P3: different managements. Effective economical
L205@P3: management requires that “new dispositions
L206@P3: [be] made every day in the light of circumstances not known the day before” (Hayek,
L207@P3: 1945, p. 524). He therefore concludes that
L208@P3: central planning based on [aggregated]
L209@P3: statistical information by its nature cannot take direct account of these circumstances of time and place, and . . . the
L210@P3: central planner will have to find some
L211@P3: way or other in which the decisions depending upon them can be left to the
L212@P3: man on the spot. (ibid.)
L213@P3: Rapid adaptation to changing circumstances of time and place requires
L214@P3: decentralisation—we can’t wait for some central board to issue orders after integrating all
L215@P3: knowledge.
L216@P3: 2.5 Prices and information
L217@P3: While insisting that very specific, localised
L218@P3: knowledge is essential to economic decision
L219@P3: making, Hayek clearly recognises that the
L220@P3: “man on the spot” needs to know more than
L221@P3: just his immediate circumstances before he
L222@P3: can act effectively. Hence there arises the problem of “communicating to him such further
L223@P3: information as he needs to fit his decisions
L224@P3: into the whole pattern of changes of the larger
L225@P3: economic system” (Hayek, 1945, p. 525) How
L226@P3: much does he need to know? Fortuitously, only
L227@P3: that which is conveyed by prices. Hayek constructs an example to illustrate his point:
L228@P3: Assume that somewhere in the world a
L229@P3: new opportunity for the use of some raw
L230@P3: material, say tin, has arisen, or that one
L231@P3: of the sources of supply of tin has been
L232@P3: eliminated. It does not matter for our
L233@P3: purpose and it is very significant that
L234@P3: it does not matter which of these two
L235@P3: causes has made tin more scarce. All
L236@P3: that the users of tin need to know is
L237@P3: that some of the tin they used to consume is now more profitably employed
L238@P3: elsewhere, and that in consequence they
L239@P3: must economize tin. There is no need for
L240@P3: the great majority of them even to know
L241@P3: where the more urgent need has arisen,
L242@P3-4: 4or in favor of what other uses they ought
L243@P4: to husband the supply. (Hayek, 1945, p.
L244@P4: 526)
L245@P4: Despite the absence of any such overview,
L246@P4: the effects of the disturbance in the tin market
L247@P4: will ramify throughout the economy just the
L248@P4: same.
L249@P4: The whole acts as one market, not because any of its members survey the
L250@P4: whole field, but because their limited individual fields of vision sufficiently overlap so that through many intermediaries the relevant information is communicated to all. (ibid.)
L251@P4: Therefore the significant thing about the
L252@P4: price system is “the economy of knowledge
L253@P4: with which it operates” (Hayek, 1945, pp. 526–
L254@P4: 7). He drives his point home thus:
L255@P4: It is more than a metaphor to describe
L256@P4: the price system as a kind of machinery for registering change, or a system
L257@P4: of telecommunications which enables individual producers to watch merely the
L258@P4: movement of a few pointers, as an engineer might watch the hands of a few dials, in order to adjust their activities to
L259@P4: changes of which they may never know
L260@P4: more than is reflected in the price movements. (Hayek, 1945, p. 527)
L261@P4: He admits that the adjustments produced
L262@P4: via the price system are not perfect in the
L263@P4: sense of general equilibrium theory, but they
L264@P4: are nonetheless a “marvel” of economical coordination. (ibid.)
L265@P4: 2.6 Evolved order
L266@P4: The price system has not, of course, arisen as
L267@P4: the product of human design, and moreover
L268@P4: “the people guided by it usually do not know
L269@P4: why they are made to do what they do” (ibid.).
L270@P4: This observation leads Hayek to a very characteristic statement of his general case against
L271@P4: central planning.
L272@P4: [T]hose who clamour for “conscious
L273@P4: direction”—and who cannot believe
L274@P4: that anything which has evolved without design (and even without our
L275@P4: understanding it) should solve problems which we should not be able
L276@P4: to solve consciously—should remember
L277@P4: this: The problem is precisely how to extend the span of our utilization of resources beyond the span of the control
L278@P4: of any one mind; and, therefore, how to
L279@P4: provide inducements which will make individuals do the desirable things without anyone having to tell them what to
L280@P4: do. (Hayek, 1945, p. 527)
L281@P4: Hayek generalises this point by reference to
L282@P4: other “truly social phenomena” such as language (also an undesigned system). Against
L283@P4: the idea that consciously designed systems
L284@P4: have some sort of inherent superiority over
L285@P4: those that have merely evolved, he cites A.
L286@P4: N. Whitehead to the effect that the progress
L287@P4: of civilisation is measured by the extension of
L288@P4: “the number of important operations which
L289@P4: we can perform without thinking about them”
L290@P4: (Hayek, 1945, p. 528). He continues:
L291@P4: The price system is just one of those formations which man has learned to use. . .
L292@P4: after he had stumbled upon it without
L293@P4: understanding it. Through it not only
L294@P4: a division of labor but also a coordinated utilization of resources based on
L295@P4: an equally divided knowledge has become possible. . . [N]obody has yet succeeded in designing an alternative system in which certain features of the existing one can be preserved which are
L296@P4: dear even to those who most violently
L297@P4: assail it such as particularly the extent
L298@P4: to which the individual can choose his
L299@P4: pursuits and consequently freely use his
L300@P4: own knowledge and skill. (ibid.)
L301@P4-5: 5The outline of Hayek’s argument is now, we
L302@P5: trust, clearly in view. We are ready to proceed to our criticisms, which are structured as
L303@P5: follows. We first challenge the subjectivist philosophy that underpins Hayek’s conception of
L304@P5: information. We then offer an alternative perspective on the nature of the problem faced by
L305@P5: a planned economic system, and we dispute
L306@P5: Hayek’s claims regarding the benefits of decentralisation. This then leads into a critique
L307@P5: of the idea that the market constitutes an efficient telecommunications system. Our critique
L308@P5: is developed by means of a formal model of the
L309@P5: information exchanges required under market
L310@P5: and plan. The penultimate section of the paper deals with the idea that change is all important; and the concluding section takes up
L311@P5: the issue of the market as a ‘spontaneously
L312@P5: evolved’ system.
L313@P5: 3 hayek’s subjectivism: critique
L314@P5: Hayek’s radically subjectivist view of the social sciences is open to the objection that
L315@P5: its constitutive category, the rational subject,
L316@P5: is by no means obviously given. As Lawson
L317@P5: (1992) has argued, a wealth of psychological
L318@P5: and sociological research has revealed that human behaviour is highly routinized, and coordinated in the main by unconscious brain
L319@P5: functions. Indeed, as Dennett (1991) relates,
L320@P5: experiments in neuropsychology indicate that
L321@P5: people act first and become concious of their
L322@P5: intention to act later.
L323@P5: For the more limited domain of economics,
L324@P5: there is the problem that the ‘subjects’ in
L325@P5: question are more likely to be juridical than
L326@P5: personal. In the main, the economic actors in
L327@P5: industrial production are firms, not human individuals. Nor can the actions of a firm be reduced to the inner subjective life of its managing director. In any large firm, the courses
L328@P5: of action taken result from a complex set of
L329@P5: practices, reviews, and decision-making procedures involving many people, and in which the
L330@P5: procedures can be as important as who fills
L331@P5: which particular positions. We would argue
L332@P5: that the economic subject that Hayek takes
L333@P5: as his starting point is not empirically given
L334@P5: at all, but is rather a reification of economic
L335@P5: theory. The rational economic subject makes
L336@P5: sense only in terms of formalised calculating
L337@P5: procedures, which, if they are realised in practice, are more likely to be materialised in the
L338@P5: accounting and management practices of firms
L339@P5: than in the brains of individuals. Economic
L340@P5: theory then projects back these practices, rational for the enterprise as a juridical subject,
L341@P5: onto a supposedly constitutive human subject.
L342@P5: The historical conditions for this projection
L343@P5: are clear enough. In the early stages of capitalism the distinction between personal and
L344@P5: juridical subjects was as yet ill defined. The
L345@P5: agent of economic practice thus appeared to
L346@P5: be the person of the capitalist or entrepreneur
L347@P5: rather than the firm. But from the standpoint
L348@P5: of the current state of economic development,
L349@P5: it can be seen that the rational calculating subject is the property-maximising juridical subject. To the extent that in a property system
L350@P5: some of the juridical subjects are individual
L351@P5: human animals, the reified subject of economic
L352@P5: theory provides an account of what would be
L353@P5: rational action on their part. But the assertion
L354@P5: that these animals do engage in such rational
L355@P5: action is more an act of faith than an empirical
L356@P5: result of science. By starting out with this act
L357@P5: of faith Hayek aimed to mark off economics as
L358@P5: essentially a branch of moral philosophy rather
L359@P5: than science.
L360@P5: But once the category of subject is recognised for what it is, not an empirically existing property of the human animal, but something ascribed to it both by the structures of
L361@P5: language and of juridical discourse (Althusser,
L362@P5-6: 61971), then this exclusion of science from the
L363@P6: study of society becomes untenable. It becomes just one more of the special pleas by
L364@P6: morality to hold the encroachments of science
L365@P6: at bay.
L366@P6: Hayek’s subjectivist philosophical standpoint has an important bearing on his arguments against socialist planning, since these
L367@P6: arguments hinge on the notion of subjective information. Despite the fact that The CounterRevolution of Science was published after the
L368@P6: establishment of a scientific information theory by Shannon and Weaver (1949), Hayek’s
L369@P6: notion of information remains resolutely prescientific. Admittedly, it takes time for the discoveries of one discipline to percolate through
L370@P6: to others. In the mid-1950s the idea of the objectivity of information had not yet spread far
L371@P6: beyond the study of telecommunications. But
L372@P6: now, when it has revolutionised biology, become the foundation of our major industries,
L373@P6: and begun to transform our understanding of
L374@P6: social ideologies (Dawkins, 1982), its absence
L375@P6: vitiates Hayek’s entire argument.
L376@P6: For Hayek information is essentially subjective; it is knowledge in people’s minds. Thus
L377@P6: we have the problem of how information that
L378@P6: is dispersed in the minds of many can, through
L379@P6: the operations of the market, be combined for
L380@P6: the common good. By taking this subjectivist
L381@P6: standpoint, attention is diverted away from
L382@P6: the very practical and important question of
L383@P6: the technical supports for information. It becomes impossible to see the production and
L384@P6: manipulation of information as both a technology and a labour process in its own right,
L385@P6: whose development acts as a constraint upon
L386@P6: the possibility of economic relations.
L387@P6: In any but the most primitive of economies,
L388@P6: economic relations have depended upon the
L389@P6: development of techniques for objectifying information. Consider the relationship between
L390@P6: landlord and tenant, and thus rent. This can
L391@P6: only stabilise once society has a means for
L392@P6: recording ownership and tenancy contracts,
L393@P6: whether as written documents or the mortgage
L394@P6: marker stones so hated by the peasantry of Attica.
L395@P6: The development of price relies upon the
L396@P6: technology of counting and calculation, which
L397@P6: can never in a commercial society be a purely
L398@P6: mental operation. Calculation demands a material support, whether it be the calculi or
L399@P6: small stones of the early Romans, or the coins
L400@P6: and reckoning tables of late Antiquity and the
L401@P6: middle ages. Economic rationality is an algorithmic process supported by a machinery
L402@P6: for computation and information storage. The
L403@P6: fact that until recently the machinery was simple and hand-operated—the abacus, the coin
L404@P6: box, or the ledger—allowed it to be ignored in
L405@P6: economic theory. But the means of rationality
L406@P6: are as essential to economic relations as the
L407@P6: means of production. Trade without a technology of calculation and record is as impractical
L408@P6: as agriculture without instruments to turn the
L409@P6: soil. Once these aspects of information theory and information technology are considered, quite different answers can be given to
L410@P6: Hayek’s problem of economic information.
L411@P6: 4 the calculation problem
L412@P6: and its misrepresentation
L413@P6: We have argued elsewhere (Cottrell and Cockshott, 1993a) that the classic ‘socialist calculation debate’ in the first part of this century took place on the terrain of the neoclassical critics of socialism rather than its
L414@P6: Marxian advocates. This had an effect in
L415@P6: defining the structure of the problem. In the
L416@P6: neoclassical variant, the problem starts with
L417@P6: the preferences of the individual agents and
L418@P6: their production possibilities. This formulation is vulnerable to Hayek’s critique, on the
L419@P6-7: 7grounds that individuals’ preferences are in
L420@P7: no sense ‘given’ to the planners. But Marxian
L421@P7: economists would not accept that these individual preferences have any meaningful preexistence;2
L422@P7: they do not, therefore, form part
L423@P7: of the problem.
